Moments like this (a sudden swell, the sound widening, a new section breaking in after a quieter one) are where listeners most often report chills, shivers or a lump in the throat. (Sloboda 1991, Psychology of Music; Grewe et al. 2007, Music Perception; Guhn, Hamm & Zentner 2007, Music Perception)
- From 0:45 it builds for 13 s, into the chorus at 0:58. A long build makes the arrival foreseeable; when it comes, the fulfilled expectation is felt as release and pleasure, and a longer wait tends to make the payoff stronger. (Huron 2006, Sweet Anticipation (ITPRA theory of expectation))

A clear beat with a moderate amount happening between the beats is what listeners rate most groovy, with the strongest urge to move; too little syncopation feels square, too much loses the beat. (Witek et al. 2014, PLoS ONE; Janata, Tomic & Haberman 2012, J. Exp. Psychology: General; Lartillot et al. 2008 (pulse clarity))
- A fast tempo (128 BPM), a neither bright nor dark sound (2310 Hz spectral centroid), in A minor, with wide contrast between quiet and loud (16 dB). The cues pull different ways; listeners tend to hear mixed or bittersweet feeling in such music, with tempo and mode weighing most. (Juslin & Laukka 2003, Psychological Bulletin; Gabrielsson & Lindström 2010, Handbook of Music and Emotion; Vuoskoski et al. 2012, Music Perception)
- About 62% of the song is parts that come back; the chorus comes 3 times. Repetition lets listeners hear ahead: by its return the chorus is anticipated and joined in, often inwardly, as if singing along; much of what makes music feel like music is that it comes back. (Margulis 2014, On Repeat: How Music Plays the Mind)
